meta.review_note: Written from the cited university extension and plant-pathology sources (searched 2026-11-14). Not yet reviewed by a plant pathologist or agronomist. Product names and rates are deliberately omitted: they change by region and over time.
meta.disclaimer: This information is for learning and research only. It is not agronomic advice. Confirm any diagnosis with a local extension office or plant diagnostic clinic, and follow current local recommendations and product labels.

classes.name: Apple scab
classes.summary: A common fungal disease of apple and crabapple that spots leaves and fruit. Severe leaf infection can cause early leaf drop.
symptoms: Olive-green spots with feathery, poorly defined edges on leaves, later turning brown to black and merging.
Dark, scabby lesions on fruit; badly affected fruit can be deformed and drop early.
Heavy infections can defoliate trees, which can reduce flower bud formation for the next season.
classes.conditions: The fungus overwinters in fallen infected leaves. Spores released in spring infect new growth during wet weather.
management: Rake up and remove or shred fallen leaves in autumn to reduce the spores available next spring.
Plant scab-resistant cultivars where possible; most major commercial cultivars are susceptible.

Where needed, protectant fungicides are timed to spring infection periods; weather-based risk models help with timing. The fungus can develop fungicide resistance, so check current local guidance and labels (many products are not for fruit that will be eaten).

classes.name: Black rot (frogeye leaf spot)
classes.summary: One fungus causes three problems on apple: frogeye leaf spot on leaves, black rot on fruit, and cankers on limbs.
symptoms: Leaves: small purple spots whose centres turn brown or tan while the margin stays purple ("frogeye").
Fruit: rot that usually starts at the blossom end.
Branches: cankers and dieback of twigs and limbs.
classes.conditions: Leaf infection usually occurs around petal fall. The fungus survives in cankers, dead wood and mummified fruit.
management: Prune out dead wood and cankers and remove mummified fruit; these cultural steps are the main control for cankers.
Fungicides do not control cankers. Some fungicides protect fruit; check current local recommendations before spraying.

sources.title: Pome fruit disease: black rot and frogeye leaf spot

classes.name: Cedar apple rust
classes.summary: A rust fungus that needs two hosts: junipers (eastern red cedar) and apples or crabapples.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on apple leaves, often with small dark dots in the centre.
On junipers, brown galls that swell into orange, jelly-like horns in wet spring weather.
classes.conditions: Spores from juniper galls infect young apple leaves in wet spring weather. The full cycle takes two years and both hosts.
management: Prune out galls on nearby junipers before they form horns in spring.
Choose rust-resistant apple, crabapple and juniper cultivars.
Early-spring fungicide protection of young leaves is used where needed; scab programs often cover this disease too. In many landscapes it causes little lasting damage.

classes.name: Powdery mildew of cherry
classes.pathogen: Podosphaera cerasi (formerly treated as P. clandestina)
classes.summary: A fungus that grows as a white, powdery layer on cherry leaves and fruit.
symptoms: White, powdery patches on leaves, which may curl or pucker.
Powdery spots on fruit; fruit is most susceptible until pit hardening.
classes.conditions: Favoured by moderate to warm, humid weather (about 15–25 °C).
management: Plant less susceptible varieties where available.

Where needed, fungicide programs typically start around petal fall and continue to pit hardening; resistance to some fungicide groups has been reported, so rotate modes of action and follow local guidance.

sources.title: Powdery mildew of cherry and plum in home fruit plantings

classes.name: Gray leaf spot
classes.summary: A common foliar disease of corn that can cause yield loss when weather favours it.
symptoms: Rectangular, tan to gray lesions bounded by leaf veins.
Early lesions are small and can be confused with other leaf diseases.
classes.conditions: The fungus survives in corn residue, so the disease is often worse in corn following corn. Warm temperatures and long periods of high humidity favour it.
management: Plant resistant hybrids.
Rotate crops and manage residue to reduce surviving fungus.
Foliar fungicides labelled for gray leaf spot are available; use local thresholds and guidance.

classes.name: Common rust
classes.summary: A rust fungus that appears most seasons but is seldom a serious problem in field (hybrid) corn.
symptoms: Small, cinnamon-brown, powdery pustules on both leaf surfaces.
Husks, leaf sheaths and stalks can also be infected.
classes.conditions: Favoured by cool weather (about 16–25 °C) with moisture. In northern regions spores arrive on the wind from the south each year.
management: Resistant hybrids and inbreds are available.
Fungicides are rarely needed, except on susceptible hybrids or specialty corn (seed or sweet corn) under very favourable conditions.

sources.title: Common and southern rust in field corn

classes.name: Northern corn leaf blight
classes.summary: A yield-limiting leaf disease of corn in North America.
symptoms: Long, cigar-shaped, gray-green to tan lesions on leaves.
Symptoms vary with hybrid resistance and the race of the fungus.
classes.conditions: The fungus overwinters in corn residue. Infection needs free water on leaves for about 6–18 hours at about 18–27 °C.
management: Plant hybrids with resistance (race-specific Ht genes or broader polygenic resistance).
Crop rotation and residue reduction lower the amount of fungus.
Several foliar fungicides are labelled for this disease; consult local specialists.

sources.title: An overview of northern corn leaf blight

classes.name: Black rot of grape
classes.summary: A serious fungal disease of grape leaves, shoots and especially fruit in warm, wet regions.
symptoms: Brown leaf spots with dark borders and tiny black specks (fruiting bodies).
Infected berries shrivel into hard, black "mummies".
classes.conditions: The fungus overwinters in mummified berries and infected tissue. Extended wet weather favours infection; leaves wet for about six hours at around 27 °C can be infected.
management: Sanitation is the most important step: remove mummies and infected canes before spring.
Manage the canopy and choose sites with good air movement so leaves dry quickly.
Protective fungicides work best when started early in spring and timed ahead of rain; check current local guides for products.

classes.name: Esca (black measles)
classes.pathogen: A complex of wood-infecting fungi, including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora and Phaeoacremonium species
classes.summary: A trunk disease of grapevines caused by several fungi that enter through pruning wounds.
symptoms: Leaves with stripes between the veins that dry and turn brown ("tiger stripes"), peaking in mid-summer.
Small dark spots on berries, sometimes ringed brown-purple; badly affected berries may crack.
A severe form (apoplexy) causes sudden dieback of shoots.
classes.conditions: Spores infect fresh pruning wounds, which can stay susceptible for months after pruning.
management: Protect pruning wounds and prune at times when infection risk is low; follow local vineyard guidelines.
Confirm the diagnosis with a lab: symptoms are hard to link to a single fungus.

sources.title: Esca (black measles): Grape pest management guidelines

classes.name: Leaf blight (Isariopsis leaf spot)
classes.summary: A fungal leaf spot of grapevines, important mainly in warm, humid regions.
symptoms: Small chlorotic, angular spots that grow into large dark brown to black spots.
Heavy infection can cause leaves to drop early.
classes.conditions: Primary infections can start from budburst; the fungus survives on infected leaves.
management: Where the disease is a problem, preventive fungicide programs from bud break are used; programs started late in the season have been ineffective.
Sprays for other grape diseases may also help; rotate modes of action and follow local guidance.

sources.title: North Carolina Winegrape Grower's Guide, chapter 8: Pest management

classes.name: Huanglongbing (citrus greening)
classes.pathogen: Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, spread by the Asian citrus psyllid
classes.summary: A devastating bacterial disease of citrus spread by a small insect, the Asian citrus psyllid. There is no cure for infected trees.
symptoms: Blotchy, asymmetric yellow mottling of leaves.
Severe symptoms on sweet orange, mandarins and their hybrids.
classes.conditions: All citrus species can be infected. Diagnosis needs laboratory testing (PCR): nutrient deficiencies are easily confused with greening.
management: Report suspected cases to local authorities or extension; in many regions the disease is regulated.
Control of the psyllid vector (especially protecting new flush on young trees) is central to management.
Use certified clean nursery trees.

sources.title: Huanglongbing (citrus greening)
sources.publisher: UF/IFAS Citrus Research and Education Center

classes.name: Bacterial spot of peach
classes.summary: A bacterial disease of peach, nectarine, plum and apricot that spots leaves, twigs and fruit.
symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked leaf spots that turn dark and may fall out, leaving "shot holes".
Pitting or cracking on fruit infected early in the season; shallower spots later.
classes.conditions: Bacteria overwinter in twig cankers and spread by wind-driven rain. Sandy soils, stressed trees and blowing sand make it worse.
management: Plant less susceptible cultivars (few are fully resistant).
Use windbreaks and reduce dust from field roads.
Copper or antibiotic sprays are preventive, not curative; follow local guidance and forecast models.

sources.title: Bacterial spot of peach and plum

classes.name: Bacterial leaf spot of pepper
classes.pathogen: Xanthomonas species (mainly X. euvesicatoria on pepper)
classes.summary: One of the most common and destructive pepper diseases in warm, wet regions.
symptoms: Small water-soaked leaf spots that turn brown; leaves become ragged and may drop.
Raised, scabby, dark spots on fruit; leaf loss exposes fruit to sunscald.
classes.conditions: Often starts from infected seed. Warm (about 25–30 °C), wet weather favours spread.
management: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants.
Plant resistant varieties (some strains can overcome resistance genes).
Remove infected plants; copper sprays help but are not very effective used alone.

sources.title: Bacterial spot of pepper and tomato (PPFS-VG-17)

classes.name: Early blight of potato
classes.summary: A common leaf disease of potato (and tomato) that can defoliate plants and reduce yield.
symptoms: Dark brown leaf spots with concentric rings ("target" pattern), often with a yellow halo, starting on older leaves.
Spots usually appear as the plant canopy begins to close.
classes.conditions: The fungus survives on infected plant debris and spreads in warm, humid weather.
management: Rotate away from potato, tomato and eggplant for about three years.
Remove infected debris and keep plants vigorous.
Protectant fungicides are used where needed; resistance to some fungicide groups has been reported, so follow local guides.

sources.title: Early blight of potatoes and tomatoes (Bulletin 5087)

classes.name: Late blight of potato
classes.summary: A fast-spreading disease of potato and tomato, best known as the cause of the Irish potato famine. It can spread from gardens to farms.
symptoms: Large, dark, water-soaked leaf lesions that spread quickly; white growth may appear on leaf undersides in humid weather.
Brown rot on tubers.
classes.conditions: Cool (below about 25 °C), wet weather with rain, fog or heavy dew. Survives in infected tubers and cull piles; spores travel long distances on wind.
management: Plant certified seed potatoes; remove volunteer plants, cull piles and all infected debris.
Scout often in wet weather and confirm suspected cases with an extension office.
Fungicides work best preventively; ask local extension which products are currently recommended.

sources.title: Late blight on tomatoes and potatoes
Late blight in the home garden (BUL 1022)

classes.name: Powdery mildew of squash
classes.summary: A very common fungal disease of squash, pumpkin and other cucurbits.
symptoms: Small, round, white powdery spots, first on the upper leaf surface, that spread to cover leaves.
Fruit is not attacked directly, but leaf loss can cause sunscald and poorer storage.
classes.conditions: Favoured by humidity or dew and temperatures of about 20–27 °C.
management: Plant resistant (tolerant) cultivars.
Rotate away from cucurbits and remove crop debris after harvest.
Scout regularly; fungicide programs typically begin when mildew is first found (one guide uses about 1 in 50 leaves).

classes.name: Leaf scorch of strawberry
classes.summary: A common fungal leaf disease of strawberry, especially in perennial matted-row plantings.
symptoms: Small purple to brown spots with indistinct borders on upper leaf surfaces.
Spots merge until leaves turn brown, dry and curl at the edges, looking scorched.
classes.conditions: Long periods of leaf wetness, frequent rain and temperatures of about 15–25 °C.
management: Choose resistant cultivars suited to your area.
Avoid excess spring nitrogen, which produces tender, susceptible leaves.
Fungicides used for other strawberry diseases can reduce leaf scorch; follow local spray guides.

classes.name: Bacterial spot of tomato
classes.pathogen: Xanthomonas species (X. vesicatoria, X. euvesicatoria, X. gardneri, X. perforans)
classes.summary: A bacterial disease of tomato and pepper that usually starts from infected seed or transplants.
symptoms: Small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves, sometimes with yellow halos.
Raised, scabby spots on fruit.
classes.conditions: Warm, wet weather and overhead water spread the bacteria. A single infected seed can start an outbreak.
management: Start with certified disease-free or treated seed and clean transplants.
Copper (often mixed with mancozeb) applied early may slow spread, but copper-tolerant strains are common and sprays do little once disease is established.

classes.name: Early blight of tomato
classes.summary: One of the most common tomato diseases; it defoliates plants from the bottom up.
symptoms: Brown leaf spots with concentric rings ("target" pattern), often with yellow halos, on older leaves first.
Dark cankers can girdle stems of seedlings at the soil line.
classes.conditions: Survives on infected debris; warm, humid weather favours spread.
management: Rotate away from tomato, potato and eggplant for about three years.
Remove infected debris, mulch and avoid overhead watering.
Protectant fungicides are used where needed; follow local guides.

classes.name: Late blight of tomato
classes.summary: A fast-spreading disease of tomato and potato that can destroy plants within days in cool, wet weather.
symptoms: Large, irregular, greasy-looking dark leaf lesions; white growth may appear on undersides in humid weather.
Firm, brown, greasy patches on fruit.
classes.conditions: Cool (below about 25 °C), wet weather. Spores travel long distances on wind.
management: Use healthy transplants; remove volunteer tomato and potato plants.
Scout often and confirm suspected cases with an extension office (national alerts exist, e.g. USAblight).
Fungicides work best preventively; follow current local recommendations.

classes.name: Leaf mold of tomato
classes.pathogen: Passalora fulva (formerly Fulvia fulva / Cladosporium fulvum)
classes.summary: Mainly a disease of greenhouse and high-tunnel tomatoes in very humid air.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces, oldest leaves first.
Olive-green to brown velvety mould on the undersides beneath the spots.
classes.conditions: Needs relative humidity above about 85%; survives in debris and spreads by air and splash.
management: Lower humidity and leaf wetness: ventilate, space plants and avoid wetting leaves.
Grow resistant cultivars (resistance can vary with pathogen strain).
Remove crop residue after harvest; fungicides exist but changing the environment works best.

classes.name: Septoria leaf spot
classes.summary: A common tomato leaf disease that starts on the lowest leaves and moves up the plant.
symptoms: Many small, round spots (about 2–6 mm) with dark borders and tan centres, often with yellow halos.
Tiny black specks (fruiting bodies) in the spot centres; no concentric rings.
classes.conditions: Survives on tomato debris and nightshade-family weeds; wet, humid weather and dense foliage favour it.
management: Rotate crops, remove infected debris and control nightshade weeds.
Space plants for airflow and remove infected lower leaves.
Use resistant varieties where available; fungicide programs are often needed once the disease appears.
lookalikes: Early blight (has concentric rings and larger spots)

classes.name: Two-spotted spider mite
classes.summary: Tiny mites that feed on leaf undersides and multiply quickly in hot, dry conditions. Not a disease, but a common cause of leaf damage.
symptoms: Small yellow or white speckles (stippling) on leaves.
Fine webbing and tiny moving dots on leaf undersides in heavy infestations.
classes.conditions: Hot, dry, dusty conditions; infestations often start at field or tunnel edges.
management: Encourage natural enemies, especially predatory mites.
If treatment is needed, choose less toxic options and rotate modes of action: mites develop pesticide resistance quickly.

classes.name: Target spot of tomato
classes.summary: A fungal disease of tomato leaves and fruit that has become more frequent in warm regions such as Florida.
symptoms: Brown leaf spots that can show concentric rings, on mature leaves first.
Fruit can be infected when green or ripe; heavy infection defoliates plants.
classes.conditions: Spores spread by wind and rain through the season; the fungus has many alternative hosts.
management: Destroy crop residues promptly and avoid excess nitrogen.
No commercial resistant tomato varieties are currently available.
Fungicides are used where needed; resistance to some groups (e.g. strobilurins) has been detected.

sources.title: Target spot of tomato in Florida (PP351)

classes.name: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV)
classes.pathogen: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus, spread by the sweetpotato whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
classes.summary: A damaging virus spread by whiteflies. Infected plants cannot be cured.
symptoms: Stunted plants with small leaves.
Leaf edges that curl upward and turn bright yellow.
classes.conditions: Whiteflies carry the virus from plant to plant; risk is highest where whitefly populations are large.
management: Plant TYLCV-tolerant varieties.
Manage whiteflies: clean culture, removal of infected plants, reflective mulches, and insecticide rotation to limit resistance.

sources.title: Managing Bemisia tabaci MEAM1 and Tomato yellow leaf curl virus in Florida tomato (IN1430)
Whitefly management, TYLCV and insecticide resistance in tomato (IN695)

classes.name: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV)
classes.summary: A very stable virus that spreads on hands, tools and infected seed. Infected plants cannot be cured.
symptoms: Light and dark green mottling (mosaic) on leaves.
Distorted or fern-like leaves and reduced growth.
classes.conditions: Can be seed-borne and spreads easily by contact: hands, tools, grafting and workers.
management: Buy seed from reputable vendors or use treated seed.
Plant resistant varieties (often marked ToMV).
Remove infected plants (do not compost them) and sanitise tools and hands.
